extracted.intended_audience: The people of the State of New York; informed citizens and voters considering ratification of the proposed Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate arguments and standards used to judge whether a general Union (the proposed Constitution) is advantageous for commerce, revenue, economy, defence, and the practicability of republican government. Focused on the practical and political criteria Hamilton and Madison present for supporting union over disunion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidated naval establishment is practicable only under union
rubrics_metrics.description: A national navy is an object far less remote than a navy of any single State or partial confederacy; different States contribute complementary naval resources (naval stores, durable ship-timber, iron, seamen) so that a united government can assemble the aggregate resources needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton argues that southern states furnish tar, pitch, turpentine and durable wood; some States yield iron; seamen chiefly come from the North. These regional complementarities make a national navy feasible and economical, whereas partial confederacies would only embrace limited resources and produce inferior naval strength or economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free interstate intercourse advances trade and commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: An unrestrained intercourse between the States will advance the trade of each by interchange of their respective productions, not only for reciprocal wants at home but for exportation to foreign markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free circulation of commodities replenishes and invigorates commerce everywhere; commercial enterprise gains from diversity of productions and from the ability to supply another State's deficit in bad harvests. This is cited as a standard for evaluating the Union's commercial benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of products stabilizes export trade and merchant operations
rubrics_metrics.description: The variety, not less than the value, of products for exportation contributes to the activity of foreign commerce and reduces the risk that merchant operations will be obstructed or stagnate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If many articles are exported, it's unlikely all will be unsalable at once; competition and market fluctuation make it easier to trade many materials of a given value than a few. Hamilton points to this as an economic advantage of a united market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of commercial interests requires unity of government
rubrics_metrics.description: A unity of commercial, as well as political, interests can only result from a unity of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton rejects the claim that close intercourse between separate States would suffice; he argues multiplicity of causes would fetter such intercourse and that only a single government can establish true unity of interests (thereby serving as a criterion for judging constitutional arrangements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Union increases national ability to raise revenue via commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: The prosperity of commerce increases money in circulation and its velocity, which proportionally raises a country's ability to pay taxes; therefore union, by fostering commerce, increases the revenue base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton uses the linkage between commerce, money circulation, and taxpaying capacity as a standard: a general Union that enhances commerce will make taxation easier and improve supplies to the treasury.

rubrics_metrics.name: In the American context, revenue must primarily rely on indirect taxes (imposts and excises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because direct taxation is impracticable here, duties on imported articles (imposts) and excises must be the chief means of raising national revenue for some time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton observes the popular aversion to excise laws and difficulty of tracing personal property; thus duties on imports and consumption are presented as the pragmatic standard for revenue policy under the Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: A single national government can make duties more productive and raise them without prejudicing trade
rubrics_metrics.description: One government pervading all States can simplify regulations and make collection more effective, permitting duties on imports to be extended and increased more than would be practicable under separate States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton notes that the Atlantic coast would be the principal frontier to guard, that vigilance and a few armed vessels could prevent material infractions, and that co-operative measures across States under one government reduce evasion—thus enabling higher, more productive duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing internal contraband and evasion is easier under national jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate states or confederacies would have easy illicit trade between them (aiding contraband), necessitating lower duties and extensive inward patrols; a union reduces interior avenues for contraband and centralizes enforcement at the seaboard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton compares the difficulty of preventing contraband in France (large patrols) to what would be required among disunited American States, arguing that arbitrary patrol powers would be intolerable in a free country and that union avoids this by focusing enforcement on a single coast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union produces economy in government by avoiding duplicate civil lists
rubrics_metrics.description: If the States are united, there will be but one national civil list to support; if divided into several confederacies, there will be multiple national civil lists with principal departments coextensive with those needed for a government of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton uses the multiplicity and cost of separate governments as an economic criterion: separation multiplies expense for equivalent administrative needs, so economy favors a single national government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disunion increases expenses through duplicated inland patrols and military establishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Separation would require many persons to guard inland communications against illicit trade and would spawn military establishments from jealousies, making separation injurious to economy, tranquillity, commerce, revenue, and liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a practical standard for comparing constitutional arrangements: count likely enforcement personnel and military expenditures that would be needed under disunion versus union.

rubrics_metrics.name: A republic (representative government) can be extended over a large territory
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural limits of a republic differ from a democracy; representative government permits a much larger practicable sphere because the people act through representatives rather than meeting in person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madison distinguishes republic from democracy and uses examples (continual national assemblies in the U.S., distances comparable to European states) to argue that extent of territory is not a valid objection to the proposed Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate governmental scope by enumerated powers and the preservation of subordinate governments
rubrics_metrics.description: The general government is not charged with all lawmaking; its jurisdiction is limited to enumerated objects affecting all members, while subordinate governments retain authority over other subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madison presents this division of powers as a criterion for judging whether a large republic will be overbearing: if powers are truly enumerated and local governments preserved, large extent is manageable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicability of union judged by communication improvements and infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: Intercourse throughout the Union will be facilitated by new improvements (shorter roads, better accommodations, interior navigation, canals) which will render communication easier and the system more practicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madison uses expected infrastructural improvements as a forward-looking standard—distance objections should be measured against likely ameliorations in travel and transport.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frontier states may be distant but stand to gain greater security and therefore will support union
rubrics_metrics.description: States farthest from the seat of government may derive less everyday benefit but will be contiguous to foreign nations and thus most in need of the Union's strength and resources; this balance is a criterion in evaluating the Union's fairness and practicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madison argues that frontier states' need for protection and inability to defend or bear expense alone make union advantageous; judges of the constitution should weigh asymmetric benefits (commercial vs. defensive) across regions.
